extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners of public relations (including PR educators and professional members)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and standards for determining whether public relations practice and practitioners qualify as a profession, including values, organizational membership, codes of ethics, body of knowledge, training, and measurement scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set of professional values
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals believe that serving others is more important than their own economic gain and strongly value autonomy—the freedom to perform as they think is right rather than conforming to organizational demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional values distinguish professionals from nonprofessionals; they include prioritizing public service over personal economic gain and seeking autonomy. The text contrasts professional values with careerist values (income, security, status, recognition from superiors). Researchers measure these values to assess professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership in strong professional organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals belong to and are socialized by strong professional organizations that provide contact with peers, accredit practitioners, develop professional culture, discipline violators, and support research and continuing education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional associations (e.g., PRSA, IABC, specialized associations) perform accreditation (APR, ABC), publish journals, sponsor research and education, and can enforce codes of ethics. Low membership rates weaken claims to a disciplinary profession; an index of professional activity (membership + meeting attendance + holding office/presenting) is one metric of professional engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to professional norms and enforceable code of ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: True professions have a code of ethics and a procedure for enforcing it; practitioners who violate the code should be subject to sanction or exclusion from the professional organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PRSA Code (Declaration of Principles and Articles) asserts commitments to truth, accuracy, fairness, public interest, disclosure of clients, safeguarding confidences, not corrupting channels of communication, not intentionally communicating false/misleading information, identifying clients, avoiding undisclosed interest groups, not injuring other practitioners' reputations, avoiding undisclosed fees or guarantees of results, and severing relations that require unethical conduct. Enforcement procedures include grievance boards and judicial panels with penalties (warning, censure, suspension, expulsion). Limitations: codes only bind members; most practitioners may be nonmembers and thus beyond the code's reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: An intellectual tradition and an established body of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A profession must have a unique, well-established body of systematic theory and knowledge that practitioners understand and apply to their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations' claims to a body of knowledge are mixed: historical texts and social science applications exist, but whether a coherent, systematic body of knowledge suffices for professional status is debated. Research, journals, and educational programs contribute to building this body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical skills acquired through prescribed professional training
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals possess specialized technical skills acquired through lengthy, prescribed education and training; such skills make the occupation a 'terminal occupation' where practitioners typically remain in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training metrics include attainment of bachelor’s or master’s degrees (and whether the master’s is in public relations). The text argues for professional education and continuing education to enhance ethics and competence. Lack of widespread advanced training undermines professional status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional autonomy and external peer evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals receive feedback about their work from other professionals (often outside their employing organization) and thus have greater autonomy to perform as they wish rather than solely according to organizational supervisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because supervisors may lack domain expertise, professionals rely on peer networks and professional organizations for evaluation. Autonomy enables innovation and forces organizations to be more responsible, but rigid organizations often avoid hiring professionals to reduce internal conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principles of ethics (will to be ethical; avoid adverse consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Ethical practitioners have a 'will to be ethical'—they intend to be honest, trustworthy, and do not do what they can merely get away with. 2) Actions of ethical practitioners should avoid adverse consequences to others when at all possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these principles as general tests for ethical decisions (e.g., media gifts, withholding advertising threats). When organizations refuse public responsibility, options include staying to argue for ethical behavior, resigning only when change is impossible or when forced into unethical acts, or whistle-blowing (which often has heavy personal cost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational measures/scales of professionalism (Grunig’s and others’ indices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers operationalize professionalism using multiple scales: a professionalism values scale, a careerist values scale, a scale for who should evaluate professional performance, an index of professional activity, and an education/training index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Grunig's professionalism scale (0–3) measured: desire to apply specialized skills and knowledge; desire for autonomy; provision of a valuable and essential service to society; recognition from other PR practitioners. Careerist scale measured income, security, status, recognition from superiors. Evaluation-of-performance preferences (peers vs. supervisors) and indices (PRSA membership, meeting attendance, holding office/presenting) and education (bachelor’s, master’s, master’s in PR) provide numeric assessments of professionalism. Reported averages indicate many practitioners score higher on careerist than professional measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of public relations as indicators of professional practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The four models of public relations (press agentry, public-information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric) differ in professional suitability: two-way symmetric is characterized as professional; press agentry and two-way asymmetric promote organizational interests without questioning them and are less professional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only professionals (with outside professional ties and autonomy) can effectively practice two-way symmetric PR because it requires understanding outside publics and resisting organizational pressures. Public-information practitioners often have journalistic ties and may sacrifice journalistic values for employer interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and pressures on consultants/agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside professional consultants can provide innovation and renewal to organizations, but agencies face client pressure to provide press agentry or two-way asymmetric services if clients demand them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An individual agency professional may be asked to provide differing models of PR to different clients, creating strain on professional ethics and autonomy. Agencies' profit motives can push them away from strictly professional practice unless professionals resist client demands that conflict with ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of professionalization: enforcement, membership, and licensing issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionalization is limited by (1) low membership rates in professional associations, (2) inability of associations to regulate nonmembers, and (3) constitutional and practical barriers to licensing communicative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although codes and enforcement procedures exist (e.g., PRSA grievance and judicial panels), many practitioners are nonmembers and thus not bound. Licensing would only restrict titles (not speech) and would require state boards and bureaucracy; many practitioners oppose licensing. The recommended path is expanded training and continuing education to increase ethical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-test items / specific professional-value indicators (Exhibit 4-1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey items that differentiate professional from careerist values include: freedom from continual close supervision; job security; having a job valuable/essential to society; salary; opportunity to apply specialized skills; having a prestigious job; recognition from other PR practitioners; recognition from superiors. Prefer peers/PR leaders as evaluators rather than immediate superiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exhibit frames which responses indicate professional versus careerist orientation (e.g., first, third, fifth, seventh items = professional values; the other four = careerist). Choosing fellow practitioners or PR association leaders as the primary evaluators of one's work scores highly as a professional; choosing immediate superiors scores highly as a careerist.
